## Why I keep coming back to this

First-year module, "How Rome held an empire together". Lesson plan is HIST-1Y-RR-07 in the department share. Every September the same thing happens: twelve-year-olds who could not care less about consuls suddenly perk up when I tell them you can still walk on a road laid down two thousand years ago. Roads are the hook. Everything else (the army, the post, the taxes) hangs off them.

## Construction, layer by layer

The textbook diagram everyone copies comes from Vitruvius, who was actually describing floors, not roads. Statumen (big stones), rudus (rubble and lime), nucleus (finer concrete), then the surface. The raised bank is the agger, with a camber so rain runs into the side ditches. Surveyed with a groma: a cross on a pole with four plumb lines.

Correction I owe my students: for years I told first years that every Roman road was paved with big polygonal blocks like the Via Appia. Wrong. Hugh Davies, *Roads in Roman Britain* (Tempus, 2002), p. 74: most roads in Britain were surfaced with rammed gravel, and the flagstone image is mostly an Italian thing. Fixed the slides on 14 Sep 2024.

## Numbers worth remembering

- Roman mile = 1,000 paces (mille passus), about 1,480 m.
- Via Appia begun 312 BC by Appius Claudius Caecus. Rome to Capua 212 km, later extended to Brundisium, roughly 563 km in all.
- Something like 80,000 km of main roads by the 2nd century AD. Some estimates go to 400,000 km if you count the minor ones. Pick a number and say "estimates vary".
- The Miliarium Aureum, the golden milestone in the Forum, set up by Augustus in 20 BC.
- Typical width on a main route: 5 to 7 m including the verges. Narrower than people expect.

## Itineraries and maps

The Antonine Itinerary lists 225 routes with distances between stations. The Peutinger Table is the one I really want to see: a parchment strip about 6.75 m long, a 13th-century copy of a late Roman original, kept in the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek as Cod. 324. If we ever do the Vienna trip Aoife keeps proposing, it goes on the list (see [[Reise nach Wien]]).

## Walking Dere Street, July 2024

Aoife and I did four days around Hadrian's Wall, 8 to 11 July 2024. On the 9th we walked an 11 km stretch of Dere Street north of Corbridge. The agger is still visible in places as a long low hump in the fields, and the line is unnervingly straight. Rain the whole way.

At Vindolanda the best thing was not a wall but a letter. Tablet 343: a man called Octavius writing that he won't collect hides "while the roads are bad". I photographed the case label and used it the next term. Nothing makes a road real to a child like a complaint about it.

## Ireland had none

The question I get every single year: "Sir, where are the Roman roads in Ireland?" There aren't any. Drumanagh, the promontory fort near Loughshinny, gets argued about as a trading post, but no roads. Instead I point them at the five great roads said to radiate from Tara (Slighe Chualann among them) and let them argue whether early medieval routes count.

## Teaching ideas that worked

- Groma from a broom handle, two pieces of dowel and four lengths of string with washers. Out in the yard on 2 Oct 2024. A class of 28 surveyed a 40 m straight line and were off by 1.2 m at the end. They were thrilled.
- Milestone exercise: give them a fake inscription with an emperor's titles and have them date it.
- Compare Roman route-building with the overland routes in [[Silk Road trade]], which were never "built" at all.

Related: [[Hanseatic League]], [[Book club Meditations]] (Marcus on the Danube frontier, at the far end of these same roads).
